questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 1

questions.prompt: In finance, the discount rate used to value a future cash flow is best understood as:
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 3
options: a government-set tax rate
the rate of inflation only
the investor's opportunity cost of capital
the bank's profit margin

questions.prompt: A project has a positive net present value (NPV). This means:
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 4
options: its cash inflows are larger than its outflows in nominal terms
it earns more than the required return, so it adds value
it will never make a loss
its payback period is under one year

questions.prompt: Which statement about the relationship between risk and expected return is correct?
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 5
options: higher-risk assets must always deliver higher realised returns
investors require a higher expected return to bear higher risk
risk and expected return are unrelated
lower-risk assets offer higher expected returns

questions.prompt: If market interest rates rise, the price of an existing fixed-coupon bond will usually:
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 6
options: rise
stay the same
fall
rise, then fall to par immediately

questions.prompt: £1,000 is invested at 5% a year for 40 years, with all interest reinvested. It grows to roughly:
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 7

questions.prompt: The Life-Cycle Hypothesis describes how individuals:
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 8
options: spend all of their income immediately
smooth their consumption by borrowing when young and saving for retirement
never borrow
only start saving after the age of 60

questions.prompt: At a discount rate of 10%, which of the following is worth the MOST today?
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 9
options: £100 received today
£110 received in one year
£121 received in two years
they are all worth the same today

questions.prompt: Spreading your money across many different assets (diversification) mainly works because it:
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 10
options: guarantees a higher return
reduces risk without necessarily reducing expected return
eliminates all risk completely
raises expected return with no downside

questions.prompt: The three classic ways to manage risk covered in the lecture are diversification, insurance and:
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 11
options: hedging
leverage
speculation
arbitrage

questions.prompt: 'Hedging' means:
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 12
options: avoiding all risky assets entirely
taking an offsetting position so a loss on one side is cancelled by a gain on the other
borrowing money in order to invest more
buying a fund that holds the whole market

questions.prompt: A company trading on a high price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio most likely means the market:
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 13
options: expects the company's profits to grow quickly
thinks the shares are cheap
expects the company to go bankrupt
is paying a high dividend

questions.prompt: A purely speculative asset (for example some crypto or a work of art) is worth:
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 14
options: the present value of its future cash flows
only what the next buyer is willing to pay
its rental yield
the value of the underlying asset it tracks

questions.prompt: The Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) says that:
questions.source: Saved Blackboard Topic 1, question 15
options: prices already reflect all known information, so consistently beating the market is very hard
market prices are always exactly right
markets can never crash
only insiders can ever make money

questions.prompt: Which list correctly names the three pillars of finance?
questions.source: Additional practice based on your L01 revision and diagnostic answers
options: Saving, borrowing and taxation
Time value of money, diversification and insurance
Time value of money, risk management and asset pricing
Accounting profit, revenue and dividends

questions.prompt: An analyst adds £600 due in one year to £600 due in two years and calls £1,200 their value today. What is missing?
questions.source: Additional practice based on your L01 revision and diagnostic answers
options: Each cash flow must first be discounted for its own timing and risk
The initial investment must always be added to the £1,200
Future cash flows should be multiplied by the discount rate
Nothing: the dates do not affect value

questions.prompt: In a simplified model, the risk-free rate is 4% and the risk premium is 3%. Which statement is correct?
questions.source: Additional practice based on your L01 revision and diagnostic answers
options: The discount rate is 3%, the full return investors require
The discount rate is 4%, because only the risk-free rate matters
The discount rate is 7%, and the project guarantees a 7% return
The discount rate is 7%; it reflects a required return, not a guaranteed outcome

questions.prompt: A project costs £100 now and is expected to pay £105 in one year. The required return is 10%. What follows?
questions.source: Additional practice based on your L01 revision and diagnostic answers
options: NPV is +£5 because the nominal cash inflow exceeds the investment
NPV is about −£4.55: the project does not meet the required return
NPV is zero because every positive nominal gain is sufficient
NPV is about +£4.55, so the project guarantees a profit

questions.prompt: A share costs £90, annual EPS is £6, and the dividend per share is £2. What is the correct P/E interpretation?
questions.source: Additional practice based on your L01 revision and diagnostic answers
options: P/E is 45, because dividends are the company’s earnings
P/E is 15, so the investor receives £15 in cash each year
P/E is 15: the price is 15 times annual earnings per share
P/E is 6: EPS already measures the share price

questions.prompt: A company has accounting assets of £900m, liabilities of £500m, and a market value of equity of £600m. What is P/B?
questions.source: Additional practice based on your L01 revision and diagnostic answers
options: 1.5: market equity is 1.5 times its £400m book equity
0.67: divide market equity by total assets
1.2: divide market equity by liabilities
4.5: subtract liabilities from the market value first

questions.prompt: A bond pays a fixed £5 annual coupon. Market yields rise. Which statement is correct?
questions.source: Additional practice based on your L01 revision and diagnostic answers
options: Its coupon must rise so that the price stays unchanged
Its face value immediately increases
Its price and coupon both fall automatically
Its price falls, other things equal, while its £5 coupon stays fixed

questions.prompt: A farmer wants protection against a fall in the selling price of wheat. Which action is an example of hedging?
questions.source: Additional practice based on your L01 revision and diagnostic answers
options: Buy more wheat to increase the same exposure
Sell wheat futures or buy a put option on wheat
Borrow more money without changing the exposure
Buy a call option and assume it guarantees the wheat selling price

questions.prompt: Which classification matches the lecture?
questions.source: Additional practice based on your L01 revision and diagnostic answers
options: A share is real; a futures contract is capital; property is derivative
Every volatile investment is purely speculative
A share is capital; a futures contract is derivative; property is real
A futures contract is insurance that always eliminates all risk

questions.prompt: Unexpected positive news about a company becomes public. What is consistent with EMH?
questions.source: Additional practice based on your L01 revision and diagnostic answers
options: The price can adjust quickly, so reading the news later may provide no advantage
The price cannot change because EMH fixes prices forever
The news guarantees a profit for anyone who buys after reading it
The old price must have reflected the exact surprise with certainty

questions.prompt: The same asset trades simultaneously for £48 and £50 in two markets. Assume trades are executable and there are no costs. What illustrates arbitrage?
questions.source: Additional practice based on your L01 revision and diagnostic answers
options: Buy at £50 and wait for an uncertain future price increase
Buy at £48 and simultaneously sell at £50; the trades tend to narrow the gap
Buy only at £48 and hope to sell next year at £50
Conclude that both prices must equal the asset’s fundamental value

questions.prompt: A share trades at £100. Your DCF estimate is £80. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
questions.source: Additional practice based on your L01 revision and diagnostic answers
options: The £80 must be the company’s production cost
The company must pay you the £20 difference as a dividend
DCF guarantees that the share will fall to £80 tomorrow
The share may be overpriced relative to your assumptions, but the estimate is uncertain
